**Trades image quality and motion stability for speed.** For drafts.
For video it **lowers Steps to this Turbo LoRA's minimum** (**3 = Express** for 4-step LoRAs). Edges get softer and motion breaks up more easily (the old value is remembered and restored when you turn it off).
With sparse attention it also **drops topk to 0.05** (0.10 for the final render), for another ~10% off.
🔴 **The draft will not match the final render exactly.** Composition, camera and mood carry over; fine detail changes.
For stills it makes **a single frame**, so it finishes fastest - at the cost of fine detail.
Use it to check composition and mood. **Turn it off for the final render.**
attention を粗くして**速くします**。**先頭 3 歩は密のまま**:
Coarsens attention to make generation **faster**. The **first 3 steps stay dense** to protect the structure; only the remaining steps go coarse.
🔴 **It only pays off at high resolution.** The gain scales with attention's share of the time, but the quality cost does not depend on resolution.
Measured: full HD 10 s / 6 steps → **0.115 higher motion consistency than Steps 4 at the same wall-clock** (all 4 seeds agree).
At 768p it reverses: **lowering Steps is both faster and cleaner**.

A RefMod is **a reference image saved in a ready-to-use form**. Pick it like a LoRA to bring back the same person or character any time.
Use it together with reference files or on its own (R2V / R2I / CharSheet).
RefMod images are **not visible to the part that reads the prompt**, so **also describe the person's looks in words** (hair, clothes, face) for stable results.
In the prompt, **`<RefMod 1>`** (or `@refmod 1` / `@ref 1`) is replaced automatically with the labels that RefMod occupies (such as `<Video 3>`). The number is the order you picked them in (the circled number on the card).
In exchange it is lighter: the more references, the faster (9 references: about 40% shorter generation).
Lowering **Strength** weakens the details and keeps only the overall feel.
Save one with **"Save RefMod" on the Reference tab**. RefMods distributed for ComfyUI (.safetensors) also work: put them in the save folder and they appear in the list within seconds.

**Drawing the same character separately always drifts.** So this makes one video where the subject is frozen like a statue and only the camera orbits 360 degrees, then pulls fixed frames out of it and lays them out. Because they all come from one clip, every angle is the same person.
**The PROMPT box is the A prompt.** Adding reference images drops in one template line each — fill in what to use and what to ignore. Describe clothing **in words**: "a black high-collar coat with silver buckles" beats "the coat in <Picture 2>".
Reference images go in the **R2V / R2I refs** section (up to 9). **Mixing different angles** makes the back view far more believable.
A portrait canvas suits this (the original uses 768×1344). **The Turbo LoRA and Steps are chosen normally in the basic settings** — nothing is fixed here. As a guide, Steps 4 with a Turbo LoRA, 24 without.

画像を追加すると**タイムライン**に並びます。アイコンを左右にドラッグして時刻: Added images appear on a **timeline**. Drag an icon left/right to set its time, **drag it out of the box and release to delete** (an ✕ appears while outside). Hover an icon for a popup with the file name, full-screen and delete. Times are stored as a **ratio of the duration**, so changing the duration keeps the same layout. Drop an image directly onto the timeline to load it at that position. Keyframes take priority over the First/Last Frame fields (not used for stills; in R2V the references fix the character while keyframes set place and time; long-form works with Motion Context ON). No limit on the number, but two keyframes cannot share the same latent frame. **Strength** is how closely the image is kept (also per keyframe in the popup), **hold** keeps the same image on the following frames, and **fit** decides how an image of a different aspect is placed (crop / letterbox / stretch)
